text: Sopore is a city in the Baramulla district of Jammu and Kashmir, India, located 45 km (28 mi) north-west of Srinagar and 16 km (10 mi) north-east of Baramulla. It is one of the largest subdivisions in Jammu and Kashmir, comprising seven tehsils and is the state's oldest existing subdivision, recognized as an urban area since the 1911 census. Sopore serves as a central business hub in North Kashmir, with its historical and economic significance reinforcing its prominence. The city hosts Asia's second-largest fruit mandi at Nowpora Kalan Sopore, about 2 km from the main town, which generates an annual turnover of over ₹3000 crore and handles around 40 percent of the apple production and sales in the Kashmir Valley, earning it the title of the 'Apple Town of Kashmir'. Wular Lake, one of Asia's largest freshwater lakes, lies between Sopore and the Bandipore district and is a major source of fish and known for its water chestnut production, contributing to the region's economic and ecological value. The Municipal Council Sopore administers the city, consisting of 21 wards and two outgrowths: Amargarh and Nowpora Kalan. Old Sopore is situated on both banks of the Jhelum River and features a densely packed network of 30–35 mohallas, including Hatishah, Jamia Qadeem, Khanqah, Chankhan, Untoo Hamam, Sofi Hamam, Now Hamam, Batpora, Ashpeer, Khushal Matoo, Muslim Peer, Kralteng, Sangrampora, Maharajpora, Arampora, Teliyan, and Takyabal, each with unique character and history. New Sopore began developing in the mid-20th century with the establishment of New Colony and later expanded to include Noor Bagh, Iqbal Nagar, Badam Bagh, Baba Raza, Siddiq Colony, Model Town, Shah Kirman Colony, Krankshivan Colony, and New Light Colony, all designed with modern infrastructure. The Sopore division includes the city, nearby villages such as Tarzoo, Wagub, Adipora, Seer Jagir, and the Zaingair belt, which comprises Dangerpora, Dooru, Mundji, Hardshiva, Warpora, Botingoo, Hathlangoo, Wadoora, Tujar Sharif, Brath Kalan, Bomai, Seelo, Logripora, Zaloora, and others, all contributing to the region's economy. Old Sopore is home to Bada Bazar, a historic marketplace that has functioned as a central trade hub for over a century, alongside Chota Bazar, a narrower market that includes a prominent fish market known as Gaade Bazar. Main Chowk Sopore, formerly known as Samad Talkies Chowk due to the historic cinema that once stood there, is the town's central intersection, linking Bada Bazar and Chota Bazar, Iqbal Market, Super Bazar, and Tehsil Road. Since 1947, the town's market has expanded at least fivefold, with Iqbal Market emerging as a key commercial center, especially known for its bustling Sunday market and its connection to Shah Faisal Market and the General Bus Stand Market. Other notable markets include Chankhan Market, Downtown, and Tehsil Road (commonly called Bugu), while New Colony, near the General Bus Stand, has grown into a major commercial hub, and Amargarh and the Sopore Bypass are rapidly developing into prominent commercial zones. Sopore was historically known as Suyyapura, founded by the Kashmiri engineer Suyya during the reign of Raja Awantivarma (855–883 A.D.), in commemoration of his name. J.P. Ferguson, in his book 'Kashmir', describes Suyya as being hundreds of years ahead of his time for his technical skills in draining floodwaters that had previously made land cultivation impossible, leading to famine; Kalhana, in 'Rajatarangini', regarded Suyya as an incarnation of the Lord of Food. M.A. Stein, in his 1899 book 'Memoir on maps illustrating the Ancient Geography of Kashmir', notes that Sopore lies near where the Vitasta leaves Wular and remains a town of over 8,000 inhabitants, having served as the official headquarters for Kamraj during recent times and earlier periods. According to Srivara, a great conflagration destroyed Suyyapura during Zain-ul-Abidin's reign, destroying the official archives of Kamarajya, though the royal residence survived and the town was rebuilt in great splendour; however, no older remains of interest remain today. In 1459, Sopur was attacked by Adam Khan, son of Zain-ul-Abidin, during a rebellion, resulting in the defeat and death of the town's governor and the destruction of the town. Zain-ul-Abidin responded by sending an army, routing Adam's forces in a pitched battle, and during the retreat, the bridge collapsed, causing 300 of Adam's followers to drown in the Jhelum. At some point during Zain-ul-Abidin's reign, Sopur was destroyed by fire (possibly a duplicate reference to Adam Khan's attack), after which Zain-ul-Abidin built a new palace at Sopore, using materials from the demolished palace in Baramulla, and also constructed a swinging bridge at Sopore. This bridge remained the sole river crossing until 1955, when it was replaced by an R.C.C. bridge about half a mile downstream; the old bridge has since been reconstructed and reopened to traffic. As per the 2011 India census, the Sopore urban area had a population of 71,292 and an area of 18.9 km² (7.3 sq mi), consisting of the city and outgrowths; the city alone had a population of 61,098 and an area of 9.90 km² (3.82 sq mi). The urban area had 37,570 males (53%) and 33,722 females (47%). Of the population, 9,329 (13.1%) were aged 0–6: 5,042 males (54%) and 4,287 females (46%). The literacy rate for those over six was 70.8% (males 78.6%, females 62.3%). Sh. Shabir Ahmad Raina is the Additional Deputy Commissioner (ADC) of Sopore, and Iftkhar Talib (JKPS) is the Superintendent of Police (SP) of Sopore.
